title: How to Cope Wisely with Anxiety
author: Donald J. Robertson
source: Stoicism: Philosophy as a Way of Life (donaldrobertson.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Donald Robertson begins with research by Igor Grossman showing people reason more wisely about others' problems than their own, a bias ancient thinkers from Thales to Galen also noted. Following Epictetus's advice to ask what Socrates or Zeno would do, he guides readers to build an inner sage, including by counter-modelling, discovering one's values through what one dislikes in others. Robertson then distinguishes mastery modelling, emulating people who seem effortlessly confident, from coping modelling, emulating people who feel fear but handle it well, and explains that research finds the latter more helpful for anxiety. He connects this to the Stoic idea that even the sage experiences involuntary first movements of fear, with wisdom shown in how they are carried. Using Epictetus's image of the two handles, he shows how a coping model helps readers acknowledge feelings, focus on what they control, and choose their response.
points: Grossman's research finds people significantly wiser when solving others' problems than their own.
Aesop's two sacks image captures how we see others' flaws but not our own.
Robertson argues our dislikes can reveal our values, which can be turned into positive traits to emulate.
Coping models that acknowledge struggle are more effective for anxiety than flawless mastery models.
Asking whether you would teach your anxious attitude to your children is offered as a cognitive therapy check.
quotes: At the University of Waterloo, Professor Igor Grossman runs a lab doing research on wisdom, and his studies have shown that people can be significantly wiser when solving other people’s problems than when trying to solve their own.
The Stoics, for instance, believed that we can better understand wisdom and resilience by imagining how a wiser person might react in the difficult situations we’re facing.
Although it’s easier to ruminate about the weaknesses and failings of others, that doesn’t give your brain good content for modelling.
Mastery modelling basically means emulating people who are perfect, or at least who perform the task confidently and successfully, without any visible difficulty.

You’re not telling yourself that everything is fine or trying to convince yourself that you shouldn’t feel anxious, angry, worried, or overwhelmed. Instead, you’re reminding yourself that you can experience those feelings without letting them make the decisions for you.

If you want to teach other people good coping models, especially children, the best way to do it isn’t by lecturing them but by demonstration – making yourself a good role model by using a coping model that works.
